newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ parliament says Peters scuffle not contempt.
newsitem.headline: NZ parliament says Peters scuffle not contempt.

text.p: The privileges committee of New Zealand's parliament said on Wednesday it did not consider an assault by Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters on another MP inside parliament two months ago was contempt of internal rules.
In a report delivered to the 120-member legislature, the committee said it had not found the evidence to prove contempt, but was "clearly satisfied" that an assault had taken place.
The contempt charge was made by left-wing Alliance leader Jim Anderton after a fracas between Peters and outspoken National Party backbencher John Banks on March 5.
Banks and Anderton said in evidence that Peters had assaulted and threatened Banks outside the debating chamber after a late-night parliamentary debate on legislation to delay tax cuts.

Peters told the panel he only put a hand on Banks to indicate he wanted to continue talking, but denied it amounted to an assault. He also admitted to having had a "small amount" of alcohol, but said he was not drunk.
In its conclusions, the committee said Peters "may consider it appropriate to apologise to the house" for the incident.
Although he apologised to Banks the day after the scuffle, Peters has not yet made any response to parliament, and was not initially commenting after the report was handed down.
The committee, which polices MP's conduct under parliament's internal code known as privilege, started hearings almost two months ago to consider if Peters was in contempt of the rules.
Peters leads New Zealand First, a populist, nationalist party that late last year struck a deal with the much-larger National to form the centre-right coalition government.
Wednesday's report called Peters' conduct "unbecoming" and not of a standard to be expected from a member of parliament.
However, a majority felt the link between the event and proceedings in parliament was "too tenuous" to justify contempt, a specific rule which has to be connected to parliamentary affairs.
The report will be the subject of a full debate in the chamber on Thursday at 10 a.m. (2200 GMT) when all legislators will have the opportunity to discuss it.
Banks and Anderton have not indicated how they expect to react to the report's conclusions.
